PLAYGROUND LESSON · PLAYGROUND · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Ladder — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the ladder — the playground’s stairway — climbed to its own rhythm: hand, hand, foot, foot, one rung at a time, all the way to the proud top.

What is this?

A ladder is a row of rungs set in two rails: hands grip the rails or rungs, feet step rung by rung, and the climb is a rhythm — hand, hand, foot, foot — repeated to the top.

What does it mean?

The ladder turns climbing into rhythm: the hand-hand-foot-foot beat is a climb you can SAY, and a climb you can say is a climb you can keep safe at any height.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three ladder ideas: the rhythm — hand, hand, foot, foot — one rung at a time, never skipping; grip the RAILS when resting; and the top rung is a lookout, not a seat — touch it, then plan the down.

Why this matters

The rhythm climb is the safest climb pattern there is — it paces the body, keeps three points touching, and turns a scary height into a counted song.

What it teaches

Rhythmic sequencing, alternating grip-and-step, pace control (the climb’s own speed), and top-of-ladder decision-making.

Words to learn

ladderrungrhythmhandfootgriptop

Say this to your child

“"The ladder climbs to a rhythm — hand, hand, foot, foot! One rung at a time, never skipping, the beat keeps you safe. Rest mid-climb? Grip the rails and breathe. And the top rung is a LOOKOUT, not a seat — touch it, look around, then plan your down-climb. Rung by rung, the whole sky!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is a ladder — rung by rung to the top!"
  2. The rhythm: climb saying it — hand… hand… foot… foot — one rung at a time. Never skip a rung; the rhythm is the safety.
  3. The rails rest: pause mid-climb? Hands grip the RAILS, feet planted, breathe. Resting is part of climbing.
  4. The top rung: touch the top — LOOKOUT, not a seat! Look around from the top, then plan the down.
  5. Play the rhythm games below and close: "hand, hand, foot, foot — all the way."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "Ladder" stands in big navy capitals inside the rounded frame, with a friendly ladder illustration below — exactly as the rungs look.

Ask your child

"Say the climb rhythm. What do we grip when resting? Is the top rung a seat or a lookout?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Hand, hand, foot, foot!" "Rails for resting!" or the lookout: "Top rung — I looked around, then planned my down!"

Out in the real world

Ladders stand in every playground frame, bunk bed and garden — and the rhythm transfers to all of them, including the stairs. A climb you can say is a climb you can keep.

Try it together

Rhythm Climb Counts: on the ladder, climb chanting — hand… hand… foot… foot — slow as a lullaby. Mid-climb rests: grip rails, three breaths, continue. Top-rung lookout: touch, look, name three things you can see from up there, then down-climb the same rhythm. Three climbs, three lookouts, one proud climber. The rhythm is the ladder’s song.

Understanding check

Ask: "Say the rhythm. Where do hands rest? What is the top rung?" Hand-hand-foot-foot, the rails, a lookout — three answers and the ladder is climbed in song.

Parent tips

Chant SLOWLY — the words pace the body; fast chants make fast falls. And the lookout round gives the top a purpose beyond height: looking, then planning down.

This lesson pairs with the Ladder flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Playground.
